hitl_conditions: Not explicitly discussed; the human remains the decision-maker because infrastructure analysis is what-if decision support without formal optimisation. Future predictive control, AI-assisted fleet scheduling and operator-in-the-loop capabilities would change this configuration.
key_finding: Gradient Boosting on 180+ real winter trips predicts electric-truck depth of discharge (R2=0.58; load, torque and weight dominate), feeding energy-optimal Dijkstra routing; a TruckMaker-calibrated digital twin with virtual interface lets planners test charger/fleet scenarios; co-simulation reproduces speed (R2~0.99). Infrastructure analysis remains what-if decision support, not optimisation.

quotes.text: A Gradient Boosting model was trained on over 180 real-world intercity trips of data collected from an electric truck to estimate battery depth of discharge based on key operational factors.

The trained model was then used to assign an estimated DoD/km value to each road segment in a directed road-network graph. Dijkstra’s algorithm was applied to the weighted graph to determine the most energy-efficient route between cities.
quotes.section: 3.3.3 Route planning and energy depth of discharge prediction

quotes.text: A DT of the case truck was implemented with TruckMaker and calibrated using real-world energy-consumption data to capture the effect of speed and road geometry on energy flow.
DB Schenker [43] pilots the case truck to evaluate its energy efficiency and feasibility for long-haul applications in Finland.

For planning purposes, the primary users are fleet route and charging-infrastructure planners. They provide as inputs the origin–destination pair, payload, ambient temperature, fleet size, and available charging infrastructure.
The current infrastructure analysis is scenario-based and intended for decision support rather than formal optimization.
